misconceptions.say: On $\Q$: it is the standard incomplete space. Take the decimal truncations of $\sqrt2$ — every term is rational, the sequence is Cauchy, and the only number it could converge to is not in $\Q$.
On $(0,1]$: the half-open end is the trouble. $x_n = 1/n$ is a sequence of points of the space, it is Cauchy, and the only candidate limit is $0$.

On the integral metric: continuous functions can approximate a step function as closely as you like in area while never getting close to it uniformly. Try $f_n$ that climbs from $0$ to $1$ over the interval $[\tfrac12, \tfrac12 + \tfrac1n]$ and is flat on either side.

feedback.nudge: Two of the five are complete. For the three subspaces of $\R$, completeness is the same question as being closed in $\R$; for the other two, go looking for a Cauchy sequence whose limit is missing.

distractors.0: No. $\Q$ is the standard incomplete space: the truncations $1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \dots$ are rational and Cauchy, and the only real number they can converge to is $\sqrt 2 \notin \Q$. $\Q$ is not closed in $\R$.
distractors.1: Yes. A Cauchy sequence of integers is eventually within $\tfrac12$ of itself, so it is eventually constant, so it converges — to an integer. Equivalently, $\Z$ is closed in the complete space $\R$.
distractors.2: No. $x_n = 1/n$ lies in $(0,1]$, is Cauchy, and its only candidate limit is $0$, which is not in the space. $(0,1]$ is not closed in $\R$.
distractors.3: Yes, and for the same reason as $\Z$: under $d_d$ a Cauchy sequence must be eventually constant, because $d(x_n,x_m) < \tfrac12$ forces $x_n = x_m$. Every eventually constant sequence converges, so **every** discrete space is complete — including a bounded one, which is the point of Remark 6.1.12 in the notes.
distractors.4: No. The functions $f_n$ that are $0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$, rise linearly to $1$ on $[\tfrac12, \tfrac12+\tfrac1n]$ and are $1$ after that are continuous and Cauchy in this metric — the area between $f_n$ and $f_m$ is at most $\tfrac12|\tfrac1n - \tfrac1m|$ — but the only candidate limit is the step function, which is not continuous. The same set of functions under $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ **is** complete.

explanation:
## Subspaces of $\R$: one criterion, three answers

$\R$ is complete, so for a subspace $E \subseteq \R$ with the inherited metric,

$$E \text{ is complete} \iff E \text{ is closed in } \R .$$

Both directions are short. If $E$ is closed, a Cauchy sequence in $E$ is Cauchy in $\R$, converges there, and the limit is adherent to $E$ and therefore in $E$. If $E$ is complete, any point adherent to $E$ is the limit of a sequence in $E$, which is Cauchy, which therefore converges **in $E$** — and limits are unique, so the point is in $E$.

So: $\Z$ is closed (yes), $\Q$ is not (no), $(0,1]$ is not (no). No sequences needed beyond checking closedness, although the sequences are what make it obvious.

## Discrete spaces are always complete

Under $d_d$, taking $\eps = \tfrac12$ in the Cauchy condition gives $d(x_n, x_m) = 0$, that is $x_n = x_m$, for all $n,m \ge N$. The sequence is eventually constant and converges to that constant.

This is worth separating from boundedness. $(\R, d_d)$ is complete **and** bounded — every point is within distance 2 of $0$ — and it is not compact, not totally bounded, and nothing like $[0,1]$. "Complete and bounded" is a much weaker condition than "complete and totally bounded", and that gap is the subject of chapter 6.

## The same functions, two metrics, two answers

$C[0,1]$ under the supremum metric is complete: that is Theorem 3.4.2 in the notes, and it is the uniform limit theorem said as a property of a space.

$C[0,1]$ under $\int_0^1|f-g|$ is **not**. The witness is a sequence of continuous ramps approximating a step:

$$f_n(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & t \le \tfrac12\\ n\bigl(t - \tfrac12\bigr) & \tfrac12 < t < \tfrac12 + \tfrac1n\\ 1 & t \ge \tfrac12 + \tfrac1n.\end{cases}$$

The area between $f_n$ and $f_m$ is at most $\tfrac12\bigl|\tfrac1n - \tfrac1m\bigr|$, so the sequence is Cauchy. Any limit would have to agree almost everywhere with the step function, and no continuous function does.

The moral is the one the whole chapter rests on: completeness is a property of the **pair** $(X,d)$. Changing the metric on the same set can create it or destroy it, and the integral metric is the standard example. Completing $C[0,1]$ under this metric is one of the ways the space $L^1[0,1]$ is built.
